blocks.text: The standard model is the collection of theories that describe the smallest experimentally observed particles of matter and interaction between energy and matter. Three categories of particles form the standard model as shown in Fig. 12.8. Matter, which makes up only 5% of the universe is composed of quarks and leptons. The fundamental bosons provide three forces: electromagnetism, the strong nuclear force and the weak nuclear force.

blocks.alt: A chart in two parts. Fermions (matter): a purple panel of quarks and antiquarks, up, charm and top above down, strange and bottom, each paired with its antiquark; a green panel of leptons and antileptons, the electron, muon and tau neutrinos above the electron, muon and tau, each paired with its antiparticle. Bosons: photon, gluon, Z and W marked as force carriers, and the Higgs boson h below them.
blocks.caption: Figure 12.8: Elementary particles in the standard model (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 12.8).
blocks.long_description: Each antiparticle is a second disc behind and below its particle, its symbol written with a bar (anti-up ū, anti-down d̄, the antineutrinos ν̄) or, for the charged leptons, with a plus sign (e⁺, μ⁺, τ⁺).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed chart marks antiparticles by printing their symbols upside down, so an upside-down d reads as p and b as q. Antiparticles are drawn with a bar (or + for e, mu and tau), as the book's own text writes them.
The Higg's boson discovered in 2012 provides an explanation for how the other particles get mass.

This model is still considered incomplete. Currently, it is unable to explain many important features of the known universe such as: (i) gravity (ii) dark matter (27% of the universe) (iii) dark energy (68% of the universe).
